title: A central limit theorem for the exodic tree and exodic matching in geometrical probability
contribution: Proves, in a 1991 working paper with van Ryzin, a central limit theorem with explicit mean and variance constants for the lengths of the exodic tree and exodic matching heuristics on uniform points in a d-ball (claimed as the first CLT in the Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley class), by Crofton's method on the generating function, and checks it by simulation in the plane.
problem_entry: {SD + IO} The long-open conjecture of a CLT for Euclidean TSP, MST and matching lengths (BHH laws of large numbers; Rhee-Talagrand Gaussian tail bounds as evidence) is entered through a tractable surrogate: the tree and matching built by Gilbert's exodic heuristic (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Crofton's method on the generating function: enlarge the ball by delta-a and condition on the new point landing in the shell; the exodic order makes the extra edge the distance to the nearest inner point and leaves the other points uniform in a smaller ball, giving a differential-difference equation solved asymptotically by an exponential trial solution matched in powers of n (pp. 5-12); the matching by identical calculations (pp. 12-13).
assumptions: n i.i.d. uniform points in a d-ball of volume a centred at the origin, n to infinity for fixed d; exodic sorting by distance from the centre; o(delta-a) events dropped (pp. 4-6); simulation for d = 2 only (p. 13); no data.
proof_devices: Crofton's perturbation of the region's volume with events E1 and E2, giving a differential-difference equation for the generating function (eqs. 1-3, pp. 6-7)
conditional uniformity: given the shell distance exceeds r, the other n-1 points are uniform in volume a - A(r) (eq. 4, Figure 1, pp. 7-8)
Lemma 2: joint density of tree length and shell distance by a Taylor expansion in A(r) (pp. 6-8)
Lemma 3: transform asymptotics by Watson's lemma (pp. 9-10)
exponential trial solution matched power by power in n (Bender-Orszag); the normalized MGF tends to that of N(0,1) (pp. 10-12)
Theorem 4 (matching) by the same recursion with n-2 points (pp. 12-13)
experiments: d = 2 simulation: the mean of L_n/sqrt(n) approaches 0.707 for n = 64 to 32,000 with sample sizes set by a +/-10% width of the 95% CI (355 to 100 trees) (p. 13); sample s.d. against the asymptotic 0.152 with 240 samples per point, called close for n > 1000 (pp. 13, 16); Q-Q plot and histogram of 1,000 trees at n = 1,000 support normality but give s.d. 0.222, and the asymptotic value is judged not a good estimate there (pp. 16-17).
positioning: After Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley, Steele's subadditive Euclidean functionals and Rhee-Talagrand's Gaussian tail bounds for the TSP (p. 3); Gilbert's exodic tree (p. 4); continues the authors' own Crofton analysis of expected lengths, S195 (p. 5).
writing: Short working paper: the abstract states the open conjecture, then the first CLT 'in this class' for a heuristic; experiments framed as verification; a one-paragraph conclusion claiming 'additional insight' (pp. 2-3, 17).
limits_future: Covers heuristics, not the optimal MST, matching or TSP, so the conjecture stays open (pp. 2-3); the asymptotic s.d. is a poor estimate at n = 1,000 (p. 16); no future directions stated (p. 17).

method_links.note: Honest-gap habit in probabilistic form: the asymptotic prediction is checked against simulation, and the size at which it is poor (n = 1,000: s.d. 0.222 against 0.152) is printed in the body, as Heuristic 4 asks.
Second paper of a programme line carried with the same student (S195 -> S829, Crofton's method).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: check the asymptotics by simulation at small n
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Mean, standard deviation and normality of the exodic tree simulated for n = 64 to 32,000 with CI-based sample sizes, plus a Q-Q plot and histogram at n = 1,000, where the asymptotic s.d. is reported as poor.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: settle an open conjecture first for a tractable surrogate
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The CLT for optimal Euclidean functionals stays open; the authors prove it for the exodic heuristic, whose sorting order makes Crofton's recursion exact.

transferable: Crofton's method on a generating function: perturb the region's volume, condition on where one extra point lands, and obtain a differential-difference equation for the transform of the length (pp. 5-7).
Solve that equation asymptotically with an exponential trial solution and match powers of n to read off the mean and variance constants (pp. 10-12).
Set the simulation's sample size per n from a target confidence-interval width, and add a Q-Q plot at one fixed n to test the shape as well as the moments (pp. 13, 16).

quotes.text: It has been a long open conjecture that a central limit theorem holds for the length of these problems.
Although for n = 1000 the asymptotic standard deviation of 0.152 is not a particularly good estimate, Figure 4 clearly shows that the data follow closely a normal distribution.

title: Deducing queueing from transactional data: the queue inference engine, revisited
contribution: Revisits Larson's queue inference engine with a faster exact algorithm that infers transient queue-length distributions and waiting-time bounds from service start and end times alone under Poisson arrivals, extends it to time-varying Poisson (by a time change) and renewal arrivals, and adds an O(n) on-line update, with timings on a SUN 3.
problem_entry: {SD; AP (banking, telecommunications) as motivation} Larson's problem: ATMs, mobile radio and network nodes log service start and end times but cannot see their queues (p. 1); entry through Larson's two observations and algorithms, which the paper speeds up and generalizes (p. 1).
key_idea: Conditioned on the arrival count of a busy period, Poisson arrival times are uniform order statistics and the logged service starts are ordering constraints, so the posterior queue length is a ratio of simplex integrals computed by two triangular recursions (pp. 2-5); the time change y = Lambda(t) runs the same algorithm for time-varying rates (pp. 7-8); an O(n) on-line recursion likened to Kalman filtering (pp. 1, 9-10).
assumptions: Poisson arrivals with an unknown rate constant within a busy period (p. 2); arbitrary service times, discipline and number of servers, provided all servers are busy whenever customers queue (p. 1); known Lambda(t) for the time-varying case and a known interarrival density for the renewal case (p. 8); synthetic regularly spaced departures in the computations (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: uniform order statistics of Poisson arrivals given the count (eq. 1, p. 2)
Lemma 1: iterated integral over an ordered simplex, by induction (p. 4)
Propositions 1-2: recursions justified by polynomial coefficient matching via Taylor's theorem (pp. 4-5)
binomial conditional distribution of N(t) between departures, giving piecewise-linear E[Q(t)] (p. 6)
integration by parts for waiting-time moment bounds (Theorem 2, pp. 6-7)
order-statistic density of a non-homogeneous Poisson process and the time change y = Lambda(x) (Theorems 3-4, pp. 7-8)
renewal-case likelihood ratio (Theorem 5, p. 8) and the on-line recursion (Theorem 6, pp. 9-10)
experiments: Straightforward implementation on a SUN 3 with n^2 memory: up to n = 99 departures per busy period reliably in under 40 s (p. 10); figures for regularly spaced departures, exponential against Erlang-2 interarrivals (Erlang-2 via Mathematica) and lambda = 10 against 100 (pp. 10-12); no comparison with Larson's algorithms and no test against simulated true queues.
positioning: Revisits Larson (1989, 1990), crediting his two 'astute observations' and generalizing them; notes that Larson also proved piecewise linearity but that the new proof generalizes more easily (pp. 1, 6); cites Gawlick's ethernet application (p. 1).
writing: Opens with Larson's 'fascinating problem' and a list of applications; the algorithm is stated as numbered steps before its proofs; no conclusion section, the paper ends with figures (pp. 1-3, 12).
limits_future: Critically depends on the Poisson assumption (p. 8); the time-varying case needs Lambda(t) known (p. 8); estimates beyond the last departure need the service distribution and the number of servers (p. 10); no future work stated (p. 12).

method_links.note: The model is shaped by data an operator already holds (step 3), and the on-line version is motivated by real-time control of service (p. 9); but the output is an estimate, not a decision, with no owner's rule and no field data in the evaluation.
A class-keeping device outside optimization: the time change keeps the time-varying case inside the same algorithm 'without adding any complexity'; the printed price is that lambda(t) must be known.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Larson's piecewise linearity of the expected queue between departures is re-proved by a binomial argument that carries over to time-varying rates.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: infer the unobserved state from the data the system already logs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Queue lengths and waits deduced from transaction logs (ATMs, mobile radio, ethernet) that record only service starts and ends.

transferable: When only event times are logged, condition on the total count: Poisson arrival times become uniform order statistics, the logged events become ordering constraints, and the simplex integrals can be computed by recursion (pp. 2-5).
Reduce a non-homogeneous Poisson model to the homogeneous one by the time change y = Lambda(t) and reuse the algorithm unchanged (pp. 7-8).
Turn a batch posterior computation into an O(n) update after each event (pp. 9-10).

quotes.text: In this analysis, no assumptions are required regarding the service time distribution: it could be state-dependent, dependent on the time of day, with or without correlations.
This algorithm is similar to Kalman filtering in structure in that the current estimates for future queue lengths are updated dynamically in real time.

title: Further results on the probabilistic traveling salesman problem
contribution: Re-examines Jaillet's probabilistic TSP: a strengthened form of Jaillet's conjecture for odd n, an LP-dual transportation lower bound, links to the probabilistic MST with an MST heuristic within 2d, worst-case O(log n) and random-instance (about 25%) comparisons of the space-filling-curve a priori tour with re-optimization, a poor average case for nearest neighbour, and O(n^2)-sweep local search (1-shift), with computations up to 5,000 nodes for sorting heuristics and a few hundred for local search.
problem_entry: {IO + SD; AP (routing) as motivation} An a priori tour of minimal expected length is wanted when re-optimizing daily is too costly or undermines regular, personal service (mail, meals-on-wheels, forklifts) (p. 2); entry through Jaillet's prime-n-only bound, an 'unnatural distinction' (p. 5), and a comparison with re-optimization from several viewpoints (p. 1).
key_idea: Use Jaillet's closed-form expected length as the evaluation engine (p. 3) and attack from several sides: cycle structure for odd n (pp. 5-7), LP duality (pp. 7-8), induced tours and the PMST (pp. 11-13), order-preserving sorting heuristics whose a priori tour equals their tour on every subset (pp. 17-18), probabilistic analysis (pp. 18-19), and O(n^2) local search (pp. 20-24).
assumptions: Independent presence with probabilities p_i, often equal (p. 3), some results under correlated presence (pp. 11, 18); symmetry and triangle inequality where needed (pp. 6-8, 11); distinct costs, 'not a truly restrictive assumption' (p. 12); uniform points in the unit square and uniform random costs for the probabilistic results (pp. 18-19); synthetic instances of 100, 150 and 5,000 nodes (pp. 20-25).
proof_devices: symmetric cycle structure of an optimal tour for odd n (Proposition 1, pp. 5-7)
dual node potentials giving a transportation-problem lower bound (Proposition 2, pp. 7-8)
f(p) as a minimum of finitely many analytic functions: continuous, decreasing, piecewise convex (Proposition 5, p. 9)
tours induced by a tree and an MST exchange argument; MST heuristic within 2d (Proposition 6, Lemma 8, Theorem 10, pp. 11-13)
solvable constant-PTSP case d(i,j) = u_i + v_j (Proposition 11, pp. 13-14)
Jensen's inequality plus a Rosenkrantz-Stearns-Lewis lemma for a lower bound on re-optimization (pp. 14-15)
order preservation of sorting heuristics transferring the O(log n) space-filling-curve bound (Theorem 16, pp. 17-18)
order statistics in the random-length model for nearest neighbour (Theorem 18, p. 19)
experiments: Random tour, angular sorting, space-filling curve, 2-p-opt and 1-shift against 2-opt and 3-opt TSP tours on 10 averaged 100-node problems, with the BHH constant 0.765 as reference (pp. 24-26); 1-shift 'usually optimal' for small p by convergence from all starts (p. 25); TSP tours degrade from n = 100 to 500 (p. 26); local search limited to a few hundred nodes by O(n^2) memory (p. 25); no run times or certified optima.
positioning: Extends Jaillet's thesis and credits Odoni with formulating the problem (pp. 2-5); builds on his own PMST paper S148 and the Bertsimas-Grigni refutation of Platzman-Bartholdi's conjecture (pp. 11, 18); uses Lin and Lin-Kernighan neighbourhoods (pp. 20-21).
writing: Abstract lists many viewpoints; surprise is a recurring note ('quite surprising', p. 11; 'Surprisingly', p. 13; 'surprisingly', p. 18); practical advice hedged ('seems to be', p. 25) and candid ('we doubt that this algorithm will be very useful in practice', p. 24).
limits_future: Open: a constant-guarantee PTSP heuristic under the triangle inequality (p. 17), even n in Proposition 1 (p. 7), the structure of optimal tours as p -> 0 (p. 25); computational limits beyond a few hundred nodes (p. 25); a priori optimization proposed for other combinatorial problems (p. 27).

method_links.note: Space-filling-curve tours warm-start 2-p-opt and 1-shift, and the incumbent practice (good TSP tours) is dueled at growing n until its weakness shows; no exact solve or certificate, and 'usually optimal' rests on restarts converging to one tour (early Tension T1).
An LP dual gives the lower bound ('a mathematical programming rather than a combinatorial approach'), but the problem itself is not written in a solver class.

The price of a priori routing (regularity of service) is measured against re-optimization as a worst-case O(log n) ratio, about 25% for random points, and curves in p; never framed as the price of a property, and p is a model parameter, not a knob.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a priori solution with a cheap update rule, priced against re-solving
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The a priori tour with skipping is compared with re-optimization by worst-case, probabilistic and computational yardsticks.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: distribution-free guarantee from a heuristic that ignores the probabilities
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The space-filling-curve bound does not depend on the presence probabilities and holds under dependence, so the tour can be used when the probabilities are not accurately known.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robustness of deterministic optima to instance changes as a stated motive
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The conclusion names the robustness (with respect to optimality) of deterministic optima under modified instances as one of two motives, about a decade before his RO programme; any causal link to RO is not shown.

transferable: Prove a lower bound for a stochastic combinatorial problem by subtracting node potentials from the costs and dualizing: the best such bound is an LP, here a transportation problem (pp. 7-8).

For a priori problems, prefer heuristics whose output on a subset equals their full output restricted to it (sorting, space-filling curves), so deterministic guarantees transfer for any presence distribution (pp. 17-18).

For local search on an expected-value objective, keep auxiliary partial-sum matrices so a neighbourhood sweep costs O(n^2), and choose the neighbourhood that is a small change under the stochastic objective (1-shift) (pp. 21-24).
Rerun the comparison with the incumbent at larger n to see whether a small-instance regime masks its failure (p. 26).

quotes.text: If we experiment with larger problems, though, it becomes apparent that the expected poor behavior is simply masked by the transition into the low-p regime described above.

The second motivation is interest in investigating the robustness (with respect to optimality) of optimal solutions to deterministic problems, when the instances for which these problems have been solved are modified.

title: Optimization of polling systems and dynamic vehicle routing problems on networks
contribution: Bounds the weighted mean delay of every static polling policy by a convex program over server visit frequencies (with KKT closed forms and a light-traffic bound for all policies), builds routing-table policies from the bound by a min-max discrepancy integer program, and shows by simulation that they come within 0-3% of the bound and beat the published heuristic tables, with a conjecture that the static bound holds for dynamic policies in heavy traffic.
problem_entry: {SD + IO; CP for the bound; AP as motivation} The polling literature analyses specific policies rather than optimal design, and no paper offers a policy with a performance guarantee (pp. 7, 9); static policies matter where a vehicle cannot see the network (p. 8); extends the Bertsimas-van Ryzin DVR line with different techniques (p. 8).
key_idea: Bound first, policy second: a convex program over average moves per unit time between stations, with flow conservation and a stability constraint, bounds all static policies (pp. 14-16); its solution is turned into random-routing and routing-table policies through a closeness condition and a small integer program with a table-length window (pp. 23-26).
assumptions: Poisson arrivals, general service with known two moments, linear waiting costs, asymmetric switch-over times (p. 7); non-preemptive, non-anticipative, stable policies, FIFO within class (pp. 10-11); the stated key assumption that server behaviour is independent of a tagged arrival, valid for static policies only (pp. 16-17); test systems from Boxma et al. and a constructed four-station example (pp. 28, 34).
proof_devices: M/G/1 with vacations decomposition via residual time, PASTA and Little's law (Proposition 1, pp. 11-14)
monotonicity in switch-over times plus the strict-priority optimum at D = 0 (pp. 14-15)
v2 >= v^2 and flow conservation giving the convex program (Theorem 1, pp. 14-16)
forward-recurrence bound for homogeneous exhaustive systems (Theorem 2, pp. 17-19)
KKT closed forms after relaxing flow conservation (Theorem 3, pp. 19-21)
best a priori server location bound for all policies (Theorem 4, pp. 21-23)
tightness: cyclic policy optimal for symmetric systems; random routing within a factor 2 (Theorems 5-6, pp. 27-28)
heavy-traffic argument m_ij -> 0 behind the conjecture (p. 17)
experiments: Simulation, 10 replications of 10^6 time units, 50,000 discarded (p. 28); Boxma et al.'s three-station example: their table 1.035 and the paper's 1.022 of the bound (p. 30); over d = 0.01-1000 average ratios 1.044 (Boxma), 1.026 (paper), 1.054 (cyclic), 1.117 (random), 1.012 (dynamic, below 1 for small d) (Table 1, p. 31); within 2% with asymmetric switch-overs (pp. 32-34); constructed four-station example at the bound by design (p. 36); no solvers or run times reported.
positioning: Against the polling literature's focus on performance analysis (Levy-Sidi, Takagi) and the few optimization papers (Perkins-Kumar, Browne-Yechiali, Boxma-Levy-Weststrate, Hofri-Ross, Reiman-Wein) (pp. 7-9); duels Boxma et al. on their own example (pp. 28-30).
writing: Numbered contribution list (p. 9), numbered questions (p. 26) answered by numbered observations (pp. 31-32, 36) and conclusions (p. 37); conjectures labelled as such (pp. 17, 37); candid that the four-station example was constructed to favour the table (p. 36).
limits_future: Heavy-traffic conjecture unproven; constructed example; random policies not optimized (p. 36); as extracted, Table 3's last row (dynamic 1.002 vs table 1.004) does not bear out the claim that the static policy is better in very heavy traffic (p. 36, my reading); open problem of provably near-optimal dynamic policies (p. 37).

method_links.note: A problem the queueing literature analyses policy by policy is written as a convex program over flow-like variables (a network flow with a side constraint, S580 p. 26); KKT multipliers give closed forms; the boundary is printed (static bound fails for dynamic policies at small d; heavy-traffic extension labelled a conjecture).

Bound, policy and gap: every policy reported as a ratio to the relaxation's bound, and the incumbent heuristic table dueled on its own example; IP builds the policy, but no warm start, solver, time limit or IP optimality is reported.
A student paper (Xu) inside the achievable-region programme, later consolidated in the sole-author surveys S580 and S185.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from the relaxation, certified by the same relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Visit frequencies from the convex bound are rounded into routing tables by a min-max discrepancy IP, and the tables are graded by their ratio to the same bound.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: tightness audit of one's own bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The bound is attained by the exhaustive cyclic policy in symmetric systems, and random routing is shown to lose up to a factor 2 before any simulation.

transferable: Define the policy's steady-state flow variables (moves per unit time between stations) and minimize a convex lower-bounding cost under flow conservation and a stability constraint; one program bounds every static policy (pp. 14-16).

Turn the bound's solution into a cyclic schedule: normalize the flows, solve a small min-max discrepancy IP for integer switch-over counts with a table-length window, then lower L_max to find a short table with similar discrepancy (pp. 23-26, 30).
Report every policy, the published incumbent on its own test case included, as a ratio to the lower bound, and sweep the parameter that decides between policy classes (pp. 28-36).

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, there are no results in the literature that propose a policy and a guarantee for the performance of this policy for polling systems.
This should not be surprising as we constructed the arrival rates so that the policy will be optimal.

title: Dynamic ground-holding policies for a network of airports
contribution: Read in its June 1992 working-paper version: extends the authors' static multi-airport ground-holding IPs to a dynamic setting with compact 0-1 programs re-solved as capacity forecasts change, size-preserving extensions (cancellations, departure-arrival capacity trade-offs, hubs, speeding) and scenario-based probabilistic versions; LP-relaxation computations on 3 airports and 1,500 flights show that correct forecasts matter more than their timing and that a practice-like FCFS heuristic costs 53-73% more.
problem_entry: {IO + AP (air transportation); LO in the computations; scenario uncertainty} About $2 billion a year in U.S. congestion costs, capacity that falls by half in bad weather, and an FAA command center run on controllers' judgement (pp. 2-4); entry from the limit of the authors' own static model S036: 'the first attempt' at the dynamic multi-airport problem (pp. 2, 6).
key_idea: Re-solve a compact pure 0-1 program over departure and arrival time slots at each forecast update, with implemented decisions fixed (pp. 11-17); extensions that keep the size (pp. 18-23); scenario models in which first-stage holds must be feasible under every capacity scenario, static and on a scenario tree (pp. 23-28).
assumptions: 15-minute periods, T = 64 (p. 7); forecasts exact between decision times (p. 8); linear costs, ground cheaper than airborne (pp. 4, 12); hold caps 4-5 and 2-3 periods (p. 11); infinite departure capacity carried over from the static case (p. 14); synthetic data: 3 airports, 1,500 flights, continued-flight shares 0.2-0.8, three scenarios with S1 at the infeasibility limit, costs 50 and 75 (p. 31).
proof_devices: time-indexed assignment variables because capacity constraints are not linear in delay variables (p. 11)
elimination of delay variables: at most 12F variables and 3F + F' + 2KT constraints (p. 13)
precomputed arrival excesses and unavoidable airborne delays for flights already in the air (pp. 15-17)
elimination of cancellation variables through sum_t v_ft <= 1, keeping the model's size (p. 19)
capacity trade-off polytope replacing fixed right-hand sides (pp. 19-21)
scenario coupling by the maximum excess delay over scenarios (p. 25, footnote 2)
no theorems (n/a)
experiments: LP relaxation solved instead of the IP, rounding mistakes expected (p. 31); all 15 forecast-realization paths for four continued-flight shares (Tables 2-4, pp. 30-33); most-probable vs worst-case forecasting vs static random selection (Tables 5-6, pp. 35-38); dynamic FCFS heuristic inspired by current practice 52.9-72.9% above the optimum (Tables 7-8, pp. 37-42); no solver, machine or run times.
positioning: Single-airport literature (Odoni, Andreatta-Romanin-Jacur, Terrab, Richetta) and the authors' static multi-airport paper S036 (pp. 5-6); the FAA's ATCSCC practice as the real-world reference (p. 4).
writing: Abstract opens with a $2 billion figure; 'first attempt' and 'remarkably compact' (p. 2); a section titled 'Structural insights'; 'a method rather than a mere bag of tricks' (p. 42); thesis-chapter residues ('Chapter 5', p. 26; 'Chapter 4', p. 42); closes with an 'earnest wish' for practice (p. 44).
limits_future: Synthetic data, LP values, no run times (p. 31); scenario model size can become excessive (p. 25); future: terminal-area and en-route congestion, special-purpose algorithms, heuristics, and trials in practice at limited scale or in simulation (pp. 43-44).

method_links.note: The model is designed so that extensions keep its class and almost its size (cancellations with exactly the same numbers of variables and constraints; capacity trade-offs with the same variables), and the authors call it a method; the boundary is printed for the scenario model.

Owner (FAA command center) and current rule (controllers' judgement) named, and a heuristic approximating current practice is the baseline (52.9-72.9% worse); but the rule is stylized, the data synthetic, and the field trial is future work.
The LP relaxation stands in for the IP; the expected rounding errors are stated but not measured, and no gap or certificate is given.

The cost of worst-case forecasting is measured in expected value but not framed as a price; the authors call the methods about equal, though Table 6 has the worst-case forecast up to about 4% dearer than the most-probable one (43,330 vs 41,669 at F'/F = 0.6, p1 = p2 = 0.2; my computation).
Thesis-lineage paper with his own adviser Odoni, paired with S036; 'Chapter 5' and 'Chapter 4' are residues of Vranas's thesis.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own earlier result's limit as the entry
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The static deterministic multi-airport model (S036) decides holds once a day; the dynamic re-solve and scenario models are framed as the next step.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry deterministic devices into the stochastic version and measure what survives
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Static deterministic formulations are used as building blocks for dynamic and probabilistic ones, and the computations measure what dynamic updating and forecasting methods add.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: computation for structural insight, not horse races
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Section 4 'Structural insights' groups the 15 forecast paths by equal values to conclude that correct forecasts matter more than their timing.
The lowest capacity scenario S1 is set at the infeasibility limit.

transferable: Re-solve a compact 0-1 model at each information update, with implemented decisions fixed as data and the decision sets updated by explicit rules (pp. 11-14).
When adding realism, eliminate variables so that the extension keeps the model's size (cancellations through sum v <= 1; a capacity polytope in place of fixed right-hand sides) (pp. 19-21).
Evaluate a forecast-updating policy by enumerating every forecast-realization path and grouping paths with equal values to read off what matters (pp. 28-35).
Build a heuristic that imitates current practice and report, path by path, the percentage by which it overestimates the optimum (pp. 37-41).
coauthors: Peter B. Vranas, Amedeo R. Odoni

quotes.text: This is a significant result, since the dynamic FCFS heuristic is, to some extent, a reasonable approximation of the essential aspects of current ground-holding practice.

Finally, the most important task for the future is to apply in practice the ground holds arising from the formulations, at first on a limited scale or in a simulation environment, in order to obtain realistic feedback which would then spur further research.

title: A mathematical programming approach to stochastic optimization problems
contribution: A March 1994 sole-author working-paper survey of his achievable-region programme (indexable systems via extended polymatroids, polling bounds and IP-built policies, potential-function relaxations for queueing networks, loss networks) that also proposes a fluid optimal-control route to policies and a complexity reading of relaxation order; an earlier, partly different version of the 1995 Queueing Systems survey S185.
problem_entry: {SD + LO + IO + CP} Stochastic and dynamic optimization lacks a unified method of attack and suboptimality guarantees, unlike mathematical programming (p. 5); a two-goal research program (unified method with guarantees; complexity classification), with a complexity map from P to EXPTIME-hard (pp. 5-7).
key_idea: Characterize the achievable region of performance vectors and optimize over relaxations that tighten as valid inequalities do in IP, under the thesis that better formulations lead to deeper understanding and better methods (pp. 3, 7-9); three routes to policies: adaptive greedy indices, IP on the relaxation's solution, and fluid linear control simulated against the bound (pp. 9-10, 44-48).
assumptions: Markov and branching bandits under nonidling, nonpreemptive, nonanticipative policies (pp. 10, 18-19); static polling policies (pp. 23-25); Poisson-exponential networks with Markovian policies under Assumption A 'For technical reasons' (p. 30); loss networks with Poisson arrivals and exponential holding (pp. 41-42); a deterministic fluid network (pp. 44-45); no data.
proof_devices: extended polymatroids with priority-rule vertices (Theorem 1, p. 14)
adaptive greedy algorithm in O(n^3) whose dual variables sum to generalized Gittins indices (pp. 15-16)
index decomposition condition (Theorem 3, p. 17) and conservation laws implying the region (Theorems 4-5, p. 18)
polling convex bound and closed forms (Theorems 6-7, pp. 25-26)
potential-function method with uniformization, proved in full (Theorem 8, pp. 31-32); nonparametric version with O(R^2) variables and constraints (Theorem 9, pp. 34-35)
quadratic-size reformulation of the extended polymatroid proving a polynomial-formulation conjecture for this case (Theorem 10, pp. 35-37)
higher-order constraints generated with Maple and PSD moment strengthening (pp. 38-40)
loss-network relaxations (Theorems 11-12, pp. 42-44)
Pontryagin's maximum principle on a fluid model giving threshold policies (Theorem 13, p. 46)
experiments: No new computation: summaries of the cohort's simulations (pp. 28-29, 40-41); loss-network comparison with Kelly on 'very limited computational experience' (p. 44); the summary widens S293's heavy-traffic conjecture with 'or for large changeover costs' (p. 29; S293 p. 37 states heavy traffic only).
positioning: Credits Coffman-Mitrani, Gelenbe-Mitrani, Federgruen-Groenevelt, Shanthikumar-Yao and Tsoucas (p. 12); Papadimitriou-Tsitsiklis hardness (p. 6); Gittins index proofs (p. 11); compares with Ou-Wein and Kelly (pp. 40, 44); Kumar-Kumar credited with an independent derivation (p. 33); fluid-model literature from Bellman to Pullan (p. 46).
writing: Thesis-first abstract; a 'research program' with two goals (p. 5); complexity and IP-analogy figures (pp. 7-9); numbered implications (pp. 22-23); a five-step recipe and four open problems (pp. 47-48); hedges 'in our opinion', 'we feel' (p. 5).
limits_future: Open: systematic policies from relaxations, bounds on heuristics' distance from relaxations, higher-order and piecewise-linear potentials, an efficient algorithm for the continuous LP (p. 48); the stochastic threshold curve only conjectured from the fluid solution (pp. 46-47); the state-space partition is combinatorially explosive (p. 47).

method_links.note: The Method 1 thesis in his own words in 1994 with every step: owning tradition and its ad hoc state, performance vectors as variables, class-keeping devices (LP over extended polymatroids, polynomial LP relaxations, convex program, SDP strengthening), duals read as indices, boundary printed as a complexity map; the fluid thesis is an early statement of the optimization side of Tension T3.
Guarantee by bound: simulated policies are compared with the relaxation's bound, the relaxation analogue of Method 4's step 4 (certificate or gap), with second-hand numbers.
Hardness accepted as the limit of exact characterization, and IP's practical success credited to improved formulations, not to measured solver or hardware speed-ups.
One programme carried by a cohort (eight PhD students and colleagues Avram, Tsitsiklis and Wein thanked) and consolidated in a sole-author survey with a recipe and open problems.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from the relaxation, certified by the same relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Step 4 of the recipe builds policies from the bounds by IP, and step 5 grades simulated fluid policies against the same bounds.
Potential functions of increasing order capture higher-order class interactions, with O(R^i) size, up to the exact MDP for loss networks.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: deterministic fluid model first, randomness second
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stated thesis that the difficulty is primarily dynamic and combinatorial and only secondarily stochastic; fluid control gives threshold policies to simulate.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: relaxation order as a complexity measure
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The order of relaxation needed for an exact characterization is read as a measure of a problem's difficulty, alongside the classical complexity map.

transferable: State a research program as two goals, a unified method with guarantees and a complexity map, and place every problem class on the map before attacking it (pp. 5-7).

Solve a deterministic fluid version of a stochastic control problem by the maximum principle to find the policy's structure, then simulate it in the stochastic system and grade it against a relaxation bound (pp. 10, 44-48).

Generate valid constraints by uniformizing the chain and taking steady-state expectations of a quadratic potential's one-step change; in the nonparametric version equate the coefficients of the resulting quadratic form, and automate higher orders with symbolic algebra (pp. 30-35, 39).

quotes.text: Ideally the approach should not fundamentally change when the problem changes.

This approach is based on the thesis that the essential difficulty in stochastic and dynamic optimization is primarily the dynamic and combinatorial character of the problem and only secondarily the stochastic character of the problem.

title: The distributional Little's law and its applications
contribution: Gives two proofs of the Haji-Newell distributional Little's law under FIFO (one new, via a generalized Burke theorem for mixed generalized Erlang arrivals with a closed-form kernel) and uses the law alone to re-derive or extend heavy-traffic moment relations, GI/G/1 and GI/D/s waiting times, Doshi's vacation decomposition, geometric-mixture queue lengths, the inverse map from L to W and several transforms.
problem_entry: {SD} Little's law relates means, not distributions, and distributions are derived system by system (p. 1); entry: show that the more restrictive distributional law can derive performance measures across systems in a unified way (p. 1).
key_idea: L has the distribution of the number of equilibrium-renewal arrivals during W (pp. 2-3); a first-principles proof and a new matrix proof for MGE arrivals via a generalized Burke theorem with a closed-form kernel (pp. 4-7); applications from the law alone (pp. 7-12).
assumptions: Stationary arrivals one at a time; no blocking, balking or reneging; FIFO; later arrivals do not affect earlier customers (p. 2); renewal arrivals from p. 3 and MGE arrivals for the second proof (pp. 3-5); batches excluded as 'somewhat restrictive' (p. 3); the law fails where customers overtake (p. 4); no data.
proof_devices: backward numbering from a random time: L >= n iff the n-th most recent arrival is still present (pp. 2-3)
renewal generating-function kernel, its Laplace transform and contour integrals (pp. 3-4)
uniformization of the phase-type arrival process and PASTA (pp. 5-6)
flow balance of up and down jumps relating pre-transition and post-departure probabilities (Theorem 3, p. 6)
rank-one inverse identity (p. 5)
expansion of the kernel in log z and of the renewal function's transform as s -> 0 for heavy traffic (pp. 8-9)
singularity matching for the inverse problem (Theorem 10, p. 11)
experiments: n/a (worked transform examples only, e.g. Erlang-2 arrivals, pp. 8-9).
positioning: After Little, Stidham and Brumelle's H = lambda G, Miyazawa and Whitt's survey; credits Haji-Newell (pointed out by Whitt, p. 12) and Keilson-Servi; generalizes Burke and re-proves Doshi; consistent with de Smit (pp. 1-2, 10-12).
writing: A lettered contribution list that concedes 'For the most part, our results were known in the literature' (p. 2); 'to the best of our knowledge' for the new asymptotics (p. 8); ends with an application, no conclusion section (p. 12).
limits_future: Heavy-traffic validity and neglected o(1) terms (pp. 8, 10); overtaking and batches outside the law (pp. 3-4); closing claim that the laws for system and queue fully characterize overtake-free systems (p. 12); no future work stated.

method_links.note: The formulation-first instinct in probabilistic form: one law unifies derivations that were system-specific, with the class boundary printed (overtaking, batches); no optimization, so the probability side of Tension T3, as card S336 found for its sequel.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Burke's theorem generalized; Pollaczek-Khinchine, Doshi's decomposition and Keilson-Servi recovered as special cases of the distributional law.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Heavy-traffic GI/G/1 and GI/D/s waiting times and Doshi's vacation decomposition derived from the distributional law alone.

transferable: To relate a count and a time in steady state, number customers backward from a random observation time: the count is at least n exactly when the n-th most recent arrival is still waiting (pp. 2-3).

Uniformize a phase-type arrival process so that transition epochs are Poisson and PASTA applies, then write flow balance for up and down jumps to link time-average, pre-transition and post-departure probabilities (pp. 5-6).
Get heavy-traffic moment relations by expanding the renewal kernel's transform as s -> 0, and check the result in the Poisson case, where it is exact (pp. 8-9).

quotes.text: For the most part, our results were known in the literature. What is new is the unifying way of deriving them and providing new insights about them based on distributional laws.
As a result, we believe that the distributional law is a powerful tool for the derivation of performance measures in queueing systems and can lead to a certain unification of queueing theory.
